statement: A 5 by 5 grid holds 25 lamps, all switched off. A move flips every lamp in one whole row, or every lamp in one whole column: lamps that were on go off and lamps that were off come on. Which of these could be the number of lamps that are on after some moves?

choices.misconception: I flipped one row and one column and counted 5 + 5 - 1 = 9, forgetting that the lamp where they cross is flipped twice and goes back off.
I thought the 16 lamps around the border could be lit, without checking that no set of row and column moves gives that pattern.
I flipped four rows for 20 lamps, then a column, and thought the column only lit the one lamp in the fifth row, forgetting it also turns four lamps off.
I thought every lamp except one corner could be lit, but every 2 by 2 block always has an even number of lamps on, and the corner block would have 3.

hints: Does the order of the moves matter? What does flipping the same row twice do?
A lamp's final state depends only on whether its row and its column were each flipped an odd number of times. Say r rows and c columns are flipped once; count lit lamps using r and c.
A lamp is on exactly when one of its row and its column is flipped but not both, so the number on is r(5 - c) + c(5 - r). Try the values of r and c from 0 to 5.

solutions.reliable: Flipping a row twice undoes it, and the order of the moves does not matter, so the result depends only on which r rows and which c columns are flipped an odd number of times. A lamp is on exactly when its row or its column is flipped, but not both, which gives r(5 - c) + c(5 - r) lamps on. Running through r and c from 0 to 5 gives only 0, 5, 8, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 17, 20 and 25. Of the choices only 14 appears, from r = 3 and c = 1: 3 x 4 + 1 x 2 = 14. The transferable idea: when moves can be done in any order and cancel in pairs, describe every reachable state by which moves were used an odd number of times.
solutions.elegant: Any 2 by 2 block of lamps, taken from two rows and two columns, always has an even number on, because every move flips 0 or 2 of its lamps. That rules out 24 at once, and the formula r(5 - c) + c(5 - r) settles the rest.

whyOnTest: Seeing that the moves commute and cancel in pairs turns a huge search into one formula, and the 2 by 2 parity invariant rules out almost-full patterns.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
